newsitem.title: INDIA: Conference to seek ways to aid women in politics.
newsitem.headline: Conference to seek ways to aid women in politics.

text.p: Members of parliament from more than 77 countries meet in India this week to seek ways to reduce the worldwide shortage of women in politics, officials said on Thursday.

Namibian President Sam Nujoma and Bangladesh's Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina will join 250 lawmakers in discussing strategies and targets to bridge the gender gap at the five-day conference beginning in New Delhi on Friday.
The Geneva-based Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), the conference organiser, said it would be a follow-up to the United Nations Conference on Women in Beijing in 1995.
"The percentage of women involved in politics is far below parity," Pierre Cornillon, the IPU's secretary-general, told a news conference at New Delhi's Parliament House.

In a study of 179 parliaments released on Thursday in Geneva, Washington and New Delhi, the IPU said only 11.7 percent of the MPs worldwide are women, down from a high of 14.6 percent in 1898, while half of the world's population are women.

The IPU, which surveyed 1,000 political parties, also said that only one out of every 10 party leaders was a woman despite a large number of female activists, and that the gap between the sexes in political power was wider now than in 1985.
"At the conference, the IPU will be advocating a new social contract for democracy based on parity between men and women in politics," Cornillon said in a statement.
But he said the IPU had given up its aim to achieve gender parity in parliaments by 2000 for a more pragmatic approach.

Organisers said the conference would debate key issues to help boost women in parliaments such as financing women's electoral campaigns, quotas for women in parliaments and the image of women politicians in the media.
Workshops divided into sessions on Africa, Arab nations, Asia-Pacific, Central and Eastern Europe, and Latin America and the Carribean will discuss regional issues.
The conference is expected to adopt a declaration on Tuesday setting out ways to increase the number of women in parliament.
"This may be the most important international conference of this century," the speaker of India's parliament, Purno Sangma, told the news conference.

Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and the former president of Iceland, Vigdis Finnbogadottir, are among those scheduled to speak at the conference, which is to be inaugurated by Indian President Shankar Dayal Sharma.

Only Argentina, Belgium, Brazil, North Korea, Nepal and the Philippines have laws requiring national legislatures to include a minimum percentage of women, and their quotas are nowhere near the percentage of women in the world, the IPU said.
India introduced a bill last year to reserve a third of the seats in its legislatures for women, but passage of the law has been delayed by wrangles over regional and caste considerations.
Critics say some male lawmakers are using these grounds to keep the bill from becoming law. Only 7.2 percent of India's MPs are women.
Also, "only 7.1 percent of all parliamentary assemblies are presided over by women," the IPU statement said.
